questions.q: Per this lesson, what is the core difference between auditing and monitoring?
options: There is no real difference -- the two terms describe the same capability
Monitoring tracks configuration changes; auditing tracks live login activity
Auditing is only available with Shield; monitoring is available on every edition for free
Auditing answers what changed and who changed it, retrospectively; monitoring answers what's happening right now, closer to real time
questions.explain: Auditing is retrospective -- reconstructing what changed and who changed it after the fact. Monitoring is closer to real time -- watching for unusual activity as or shortly after it happens.

questions.q: A compliance reviewer asks who changed the Field-Level Security setting on a sensitive field, and when. Which feature actually answers that?
options: Setup Audit Trail
Field History Tracking / Field Audit Trail
Real-Time Event Monitoring
Transaction Security Policies
questions.explain: Setup Audit Trail records administrative/configuration changes made in Setup, such as a Field-Level Security setting being edited -- it does not track record-level field value changes, which is a separate feature.

questions.q: What does Field History Tracking / Field Audit Trail actually track, as distinct from Setup Audit Trail?
options: Which users are currently logged into the org
Changes to the actual values of specific fields on individual records over time, including what the value was before a change
API call volume by integration user
Which reports have been exported in the last 24 hours
questions.explain: Field History Tracking (and Shield's extended Field Audit Trail) tracks the history of a field's actual value on a specific record over time -- a different question than Setup Audit Trail's "what administrative setting changed."

questions.q: Why does this lesson introduce Event Monitoring and Transaction Security only briefly here, deferring the deep mechanics to Chapter 2?
options: Because they are legacy features Salesforce is retiring
Because Event Monitoring and Transaction Security Policies don't actually exist on the platform

Because this lesson's purpose is to establish monitoring/auditing as a deliberately designed layer with real named tools, before going deep on Event Monitoring's and Transaction Security's specific mechanics later
Because those features require a different lesson's screenshot policy
questions.explain: This lesson is explicitly an overview that names the sixth defense-in-depth layer (monitoring/response) and its tools, setting up Chapter 2's dedicated, deeper lesson on Event Monitoring and Transaction Security specifically.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue that "we'll figure out logging later" is not an acceptable design decision for an architect?
options: Because logging is required by every Salesforce license regardless of design choices
Because monitoring is only relevant to healthcare-industry orgs
Because Setup Audit Trail cannot be enabled after an org has been live for more than 90 days

Because leaving the monitoring/response layer undesigned means a failure at any other layer can go undetected, which is functionally indistinguishable from no failure happening at all -- until it isn't
questions.explain: An undesigned monitoring layer means a failure elsewhere in the defense-in-depth stack can go completely undetected -- the whole point of treating monitoring as a designed layer, per Lesson 3, is to catch failures instead of discovering them only after real damage has compounded.
